deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is the middle page of an administrative report (Gutachten) addressed to the 'Hohes Curatorium' of the University of Göttingen. The report answers a ministerial rescript, which the earlier and later pages show concerns General J. J. Baeyer's proposal (1861-62) for a central European arc measurement (Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung).

The argument on this page runs as follows.
(1) For determining longitude differences, the electric telegraph is a new instrument fully suited to the purpose and worth exploiting.
(2) Formal request: the Curatorium should order (a) a telegraphic connection between the Göttingen observatory and the Göttingen telegraph station, and (b) the purchase of a telegraphic registering apparatus (a chronograph).
(3) Justification for (b): such an apparatus has become almost indispensable for all finer astronomical observations. With improvements specified by P. A. Hansen (Gotha), the mechanic Ausfeld in Gotha now supplies it at the much reduced price of 200 Thaler. It would therefore be urgently needed by the Royal Observatory in any case.
(4) This would make it possible to determine longitude differences between Göttingen and other observatories. Here the words 'nach dem vom General Baeyer gemachten Vorschlage' are struck out.

The following page continues: telegraph-connected observatories, a second portable registering apparatus, and the need to combine longitude with latitude and gravity (pendulum) determinations.

The underlying scientific method is the telegraphic determination of longitude: clock signals or star transits are compared by telegraph, and a chronograph registers them. That method is entirely standard for the period.

results.what: Proposal to connect the Göttingen observatory to the telegraph network and buy a Hansen/Ausfeld registering chronograph for telegraphic longitude-difference determinations, in support of Baeyer's arc-measurement project
results.usually_credited_to: US Coast Survey (Walker, Bond, Locke, 1840s); in Europe Struve, Airy and others in the 1850s; the Gotha chronograph to P. A. Hansen and Ausfeld

deep.surprise_reason: This is an institutional report about acquiring instruments, with no mathematical content. Its authorship may be collective (Göttingen faculty, e.g. Weber or Riemann as signatories), and its content was standard practice in the 1860s.
transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'daher unserem Erachten' should most likely read 'daher unseres Erachtens' (the idiomatic phrase, consistent with the image).
Line 2: 'elektrischen Telegraphen' is underlined in the manuscript, and pencil diagonal lines cross the first four lines (likely editorial marks, not deletions).
Last lines: the strikeout covers 'nach' and the whole phrase 'dem vom General Baeyer gemachten Vorschlage'. The transcription's rendering is correct.
